title: Rufus and the Cosmic Surprise
markdown:
Wizard Rufus was a man of sharp plans and a wardrobe that often looked as if it had tangled with a grumpy badger and barely escaped. His tower, however, was a palace of neatness: spell scrolls sorted like treasures, potions gleaming in their places. His mind was a fortress of order, a castle of catalogued knowledge.

He stood on the edge of a most important task: watching the Whispering Comet line up in a truly amazing way. He needed a familiar—not just any friend, but one whose senses could hum with the stars, whose eyes could shine like the night sky, whose spirit could sing the old songs of the heavens. The comet was a wild sparkling thing, unpredictable magic. Alignment was a big deal. Everyday things felt a little closer to dreams.

So he went to the Sunstone Market, tucked high in the mountains of Aethelgard: a noisy jumbled symphony. Villages clung to rocky sides, windows like a thousand curious eyes. Rope bridges swayed like dizzy spiderwebs, groaning. Pine and smoky nuts, a hint of strange bubbling stews. The market pulsed like a happy heartbeat against the mountain’s chest. Stalls overflowed with shiny trinkets and puzzling gadgets that whirred and clicked. Tiny bells on awnings tinkled. Sellers shouted.

A boy sold roasted chestnuts from a pan that hissed like a small dragon. A woman in a yellow shawl measured ribbon by the arm. Somewhere a goat complained about the price of apples. Rufus wrote none of this on his list. Lists, in his view, were for important things.

“Now, Sprig.” Spectacles up; they slid, wire frames a little bent. “We must be careful. I have my list, neat and tidy. A familiar fast, before the first star.”

Sprig, goblin helper, moss after spring rain, clever sparkle in his eyes, nodded. Pointed ears twitched at the din. “Indeed, Master Rufus. Though ‘careful’ might be a strong word. More like a playful whirlwind of curious possibilities.” A clawed hand at the happy chaos: acrobatic sellers juggling glowing balls, potions that changed colour when you looked away.

Rufus puffed his chest, robes billowing. “Nonsense. The perfect familiar without wasting a moment. Precision and purpose.” He smoothed his beard; a little feather stuck, waving like a tiny proud flag.

Their search led to a stall of silks that shimmered and changed, captured moonlight. Behind it a goblin with eyes like polished jet, fingers a blur, silver bracelets, copper rings. Grizelda: surprising timing, wonderfully odd wares, a rainbow of things that broke the rules of sense.

“Greetings, sky-watcher!” A thousand tiny coins jingling. Crescent-moon smile, a gold tooth. “What wondrous thing does your heart sing for, that your spirit might fly high?”

Rufus tapped the list with an ink-stained finger. “A companion. A creature of the air whose songs echo the music of the stars. A songbird that sings of the cosmos. One that can sing the constellations into being.”

Fingers flew. “Ah, a singer! You need this!” A flourish, beads scattering, and she held out a rock. A very grumpy-looking grey rock, potato-sized, snoring little puffs of dust.

Rufus stared. Sprig blinked, head tilted.

“That is,” slowly, organised mind bubbling like an uncorked potion, “a rock.”

“The best grumpy rock in all of Oakhaven!” Affectionate pat. “Its snores, loud enough, can help any asteroid fall peacefully asleep. Quiet nights!”

A small quiet sigh, dry leaves. “Not a bird. Not a singer. A very peculiar rock with rather loud snores.” He scribbled: Rock — loud snores. Odd. Could it be made louder?

He almost put the rock back. Then he did not. It sat in his palm like a stubborn fact. Sprig, who collected stubborn facts the way other goblins collected buttons, looked pleased.

On they went, cinnamon and baked apples from a bakery. The comet closer, faint shimmer in the darkening sky. A tiny wobble in the organised mind. “Next: a creature whose eyes see through the deepest dark, faraway star clouds, not specks of dust. An owl, perhaps. Bright eyes for hidden pictures in the dark sky.”

Grizelda, somehow at the next stall of shimmering crystals, beamed. “Bright eyes for the dark? Just the thing!” Dramatic unfurling of velvet stitched with tiny silver stars: a polished obsidian disc pulsing so bright it stole colour from the market.

Rufus jumped, shielded his eyes. Sleeve brushed wind chimes, a startled ring. “Goodness gracious! Not for seeing in the dark. For making a light so bright you can’t see. A portable sunbeam!” Glare bounced off wet stones. Everyone squinted. A cat under a cart flattened its ears and left in a hurry that suggested it had opinions about astronomy.

Sprig watched her hands: incredibly quick. Eyes darted not at Rufus’s flustered face but at the sky, the ever-brightening comet. She subtly rearranged peculiar little objects into a strange thoughtful order.

“Master Rufus.” Low rumble through the noise. “Perhaps the trader isn’t unhelpful, but confusingly helpful. Gifts the opposite of what you ask, useful in a different way.”

Rufus felt a spark of competition. Capable wizard, not easily tricked by market games. Funny, annoying challenge. List-making buzzing. “Confusingly helpful? The only thing confusing is the quality of the goods. One more try, Grizelda. A familiar to track the comet’s tiny movements. Sharp senses for little details. Something that can find what’s almost invisible.” Firm resolve, mind racing through hard-to-see parts of mapping stars.

Grizelda clapped. “A finder! You shall have it!” From under the counter, a shimmering impossibly tangled ball of colourful yarn, wiggling by itself: sapphire, emerald, amethyst in a wild embrace.

Shoulders drooped. “Yarn. A ball of yarn.” Sprig tilted his head, thoughtful. “Not a familiar. A craft project gone terribly wrong. It looks as if it’s trying to get away.”

A thread of purple escaped and wound around Rufus’s thumb. He unwound it with the patience of a man who alphabetised his spoons. The yarn, unimpressed, wound the other way.

Sky a deep velvety purple, bruised plums, first brave stars. The comet growing, ghostly light on the mountain tops. Real worry, like missing spell ingredients. Perfect plans messed up by a goblin who gave the exact opposite. He pictured the tower open to the comet’s wild energy, instruments unprotected. His astrolabe, his charts, the little brass clock that only told the truth on Tuesdays—all of it sitting under a sky about to misbehave.

Then Sprig’s eyes widened in the faint comet-light. Grumpy rock, low rumble. Dazzling disc, still faintly glowing. Writhing yarn, a messy tangle of possibilities. Rufus about to launch into star-mapping and special tools.

“Master Rufus.” Calm, steady, market fading. “You said you need to chart the comet. What about protecting your workshop from its alignment? The energy can be frisky. Bounce and spill, especially this close.”

Mouth slightly open. Frisky. The still quiet rock: snores to lull. The sunstone’s blinding light, so bothersome, could push away something bright and energetic. The yarn: a web, a barrier.

He turned the three things over in his mind the way he turned pages: rock, light, tangle. Not a bird. Not an owl. Not a finder. Three answers to a question he had not written down.

“You mean Grizelda wasn’t giving me the wrong familiar. She was giving me the right tools for a different, just as important, job?”

Grizelda, polishing rather dull spectacles with silk, looked up and winked. “A wizard getting ready for the Whispering Comet might want to shield his delicate instruments. Energy blocking. A sound-soother for wobbly vibrations. A strong barrier of the toughest threads. Smart, when the sky is about to put on a big show.”

Warmth nicer than worry. His plan had been so focused on charting, on watching, he had missed the simple practical need for protection. Competition faded into understanding and a little amused self-pity. He looked at Sprig with huge thanks. The helper’s idea shone brighter than any star.

“Well done, Sprig. More understanding than any familiar I might have picked from this jumbled market. You see the bigger picture. The hidden links.”

He turned back, new purpose. He did not need a cosmic singer or a star-gazer. He had Sprig, an adaptable mind, Grizelda’s surprisingly useful supplies. He even had a grumpy rock that could lull.

Then: a small ordinary creature on a sack of dried herbs. A field mouse, ears twitching with keen attention, eyes of deep quiet wisdom. Not grand, not flashy, would not sing heavenly songs. Watched everything with silent smart focus: hustle, footsteps, clatter. It watched the rock, the disc, the yarn. It watched Rufus’s list, which had a smudge where *songbird* used to be.

“That one.” Soft. “That little fellow. A keen observer. A quiet watcher of details.”

The mouse hopped onto his outstretched finger, warm, tiny heart a steady comforting rhythm. No grand powers. A steady presence.

Grizelda wrapped the rock in brown paper that still snored. She wrapped the disc in velvet that leaked a little daylight. She did not wrap the yarn; it wrapped itself, sulking, into a tidy knot that would not stay tidy.

As the comet began its real descent, bright streaks of ethereal light, Rufus, Sprig, and the mouse—whom Rufus decided to call Flicker—headed for the tower. Grizelda watched them go, faint smile, stall of perfectly wrong items fading into the colourful scene.

On the rope bridge the mountain wind tried to steal the list. Sprig caught it. Rufus did not ask for it back. Flicker rode in a pocket, a small warm comma against the wizard’s ribs.

They reached the tower as the first true blaze of comet-light washed the stones. Rufus set the rock by the window where the glass hummed. He hung the disc so its glare faced the sky, not the charts. He strung the yarn from beam to beam until the workshop wore a messy glittering web. Flicker sat on a ledger and watched. Sprig stood in the doorway, moss-green and sure.

The comet blazed. Nobody sang the constellations. The rock, in its paper, snored anyway. Instruments stayed put. Rufus, robes still a little rumpled, felt quiet happiness that did not need a list.
characters: Rufus (wizard), Sprig (goblin), Grizelda (goblin trader), Flicker (field mouse)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing fantasy story for middle-grade readers
